chapters.title: Sonnets 1–17: The Procreation Sonnets
paragraphs: Sonnet 1

We want the most beautiful creatures to have children, so that beauty’s rose never dies out. That way, as the older flower withers with time, its young heir can carry on its memory. But you are engaged only to your own bright eyes. You feed the flame of your light with fuel made from your own self. You create a famine where there is plenty, and you are your own enemy, far too cruel to your sweet self. You are now the world’s fresh ornament and the only messenger of the bright spring. Yet you bury your future inside your own bud. You are a young miser who wastes everything by hoarding it. Take pity on the world, or else be a glutton who eats what the world is owed, swallowing it between yourself and the grave.
Sonnet 2

When forty winters lay siege to your forehead and dig deep trenches in the field of your beauty, the proud uniform of your youth, so admired now, will be a ragged garment worth very little. Then someone will ask where all your beauty has gone, where all the treasure of your vigorous days is. To answer that it lies inside your own deep, sunken eyes would be a shame that eats everything, and empty, wasteful praise. How much more praise would the use of your beauty earn if you could answer, ‘This beautiful child of mine will settle my account and excuse me when I’m old.’ That would prove his beauty came to him from you. This would be like being made new when you are old. You would see your blood run warm when you feel it running cold.
Sonnet 3

Look in your mirror and tell the face you see that it’s time for it to make another face. If you don’t renew its fresh condition now, you cheat the world and deny some woman the blessing of motherhood. For where is there a woman so beautiful that her unplowed womb would refuse your farming? Or what man is so foolish that he would become the tomb of his own self-love and cut off his descendants? You are your mother’s mirror. In you she calls back the lovely April of her youth. In the same way, through the windows of your old age you will see this golden time of yours, despite your wrinkles. But if you live in a way that means you won’t be remembered, then die single, and your image will die with you.
Sonnet 4

Wasteful, lovely one, why do you spend the inheritance of your beauty on yourself alone? Nature’s will gives nothing away for good; it only lends. Being generous, she lends to those who are generous too. So, beautiful miser, why do you misuse the generous gift you were given to pass on? You are a moneylender who makes no profit. Why do you use such a great sum of sums and still can’t make a living? Since you do business only with yourself, you cheat your own sweet self. So when Nature calls you to go, what acceptable account can you leave behind? Your unused beauty must be buried in the tomb with you. If it were used, it would live on as the executor of your estate.
Sonnet 5

The hours that gently shaped that lovely face, which every eye lingers on, will become tyrants to that same face. They will make ugly what is now beautiful beyond all others. Time never rests, and it leads summer on to hideous winter and destroys it there. The sap is stopped by frost, the vigorous leaves are all gone, and beauty is covered in snow, with bareness everywhere. Then, if summer’s essence were not left behind, a liquid prisoner locked in walls of glass, beauty and everything it creates would be lost. Nothing of it would remain, not even a memory of what it was. But flowers that have been distilled into perfume lose only their outward show when winter comes. Their essence still lives on, sweet.
Sonnet 6

So don’t let winter’s rough hand destroy the summer in you before you have been distilled. Make some bottle sweet. Fill some place with the treasure of your beauty before that beauty kills itself. Lending at interest is not forbidden when it makes happy those who willingly pay back the loan. That’s what it would be for you to breed another you. You would be ten times happier if each one gave you ten for one. Ten of you would be ten times happier than you are now, if ten of your children each copied you ten times over. Then what could Death do if you died, when you would still be living on in your descendants? Don’t be stubborn and self-willed. You are far too beautiful to be Death’s prize and make worms your heirs.
Sonnet 7

Look! In the east, when the gracious sun lifts up his burning head, every eye down below pays homage to his newly appearing sight. They serve his sacred majesty with their looks. And when he has climbed the steep hill of heaven, looking like a strong young man in the prime of life, mortal eyes still adore his beauty. They follow him on his golden journey. But when he reaches the highest point and, in his weary chariot, staggers away from the day like a feeble old man, those eyes, so dutiful before, now turn away from his low path and look somewhere else. It’s the same with you. You are now passing beyond your noon. You will die with no one looking at you unless you have a son.
Sonnet 8

You are music to listen to, so why does music make you sad? Sweet things don’t fight with sweet things, and joy delights in joy. Why do you love something you don’t receive gladly? Or why do you receive with pleasure what annoys you? If the true harmony of well-tuned notes, married together in chords, offends your ear, they are only scolding you sweetly. You are ruining, by staying single, the harmony you ought to play your part in. Notice how one string, like a sweet husband to another, sounds in harmony with it, each striking the other in mutual order. They are like a father, a child and a happy mother, who all sing one pleasing note together. Their wordless song, many voices that seem to be one, sings this to you: ‘You, alone, will amount to nothing.’
Sonnet 9

Is it because you are afraid of making a widow cry that you use yourself up in a single life? Ah! If you happen to die without children, the world will mourn you like a wife who has lost her mate. The world will be your widow and keep weeping that you left no copy of yourself behind. Meanwhile every ordinary widow can keep her husband’s likeness in mind by looking into her children’s eyes. Look, whatever a spendthrift wastes in the world only changes hands, because the world still gets to enjoy it. But beauty that is wasted comes to an end in this world. By keeping it unused, its owner destroys it. There is no love for others in the heart of someone who commits such murderous shame against himself.
Sonnet 10

Shame on you! Admit that you love no one, since you are so careless about your own future. Grant, if you like, that many people love you. But it is perfectly clear that you love no one. You are so possessed by murderous hate that you don’t hesitate to plot against yourself. You are trying to ruin that beautiful house, your body and your family line, when repairing it should be your chief desire. Oh, change your way of thinking, so that I can change my opinion of you! Should hate have a finer home than gentle love? Be as gracious and kind as you look. Or at least prove kind-hearted toward yourself. Make yourself another self, out of love for me, so that beauty can still live in your children or in you.
Sonnet 11

As fast as you fade, you will grow just as fast again in one of your children, out of what you give up. And that fresh blood which you give while young, you can call your own when you move on from youth. In this lies wisdom, beauty and increase. Without it there is only folly, old age and cold decay. If everyone thought the way you do, the generations would stop, and sixty years would wipe out the world. Let those whom Nature didn’t make for breeding, the harsh, ugly and crude, die without children. Look, to those she gave the most, she gave you even more. You should cherish that generous gift by being generous with it. She carved you to be her seal, and by that she meant that you should print more copies, not let the original die.
Sonnet 12

I count the strokes of the clock that tells the time, and I see the splendid day sink into hideous night. I see the violet past its prime, and black curls all turned silver with white. I see tall trees stripped of their leaves, trees that once sheltered the herd from the heat. I see summer’s green crops all bound up in sheaves, carried on the bier like a corpse with a white, bristly beard. When I see all this, I start to wonder about your beauty. I think how you too must go among the things that time destroys. Sweet and beautiful things abandon themselves, and they die as fast as they see others grow. Nothing can defend against Time’s scythe except children, who can defy him when he takes you away.
Sonnet 13

Oh, if only you were yourself forever! But, my love, you belong to yourself only as long as you live here. You should prepare for this coming end and give your sweet likeness to someone else. Then the beauty you hold only on lease would never expire. You would be yourself again after your own death, when your sweet children carried your sweet looks. Who lets so beautiful a house fall into ruin, when careful management could keep it up with honor against the stormy blasts of winter and the barren rage of death’s eternal cold? Oh, no one but wasters. My dear love, you know you had a father. Let your son be able to say the same.
Sonnet 14

I don’t pluck my judgments from the stars. And yet I think I know astrology, though not to predict good or bad luck, plagues, famines or what kind of seasons are coming. I can’t tell fortunes down to the minute, assigning to each one his thunder, rain and wind. Nor can I tell princes whether things will go well, from frequent signs I find in the heavens. But I get my knowledge from your eyes. In those constant stars I read this lesson: ‘Truth and beauty will thrive together if you would turn from yourself to producing heirs.’ Otherwise, this is what I predict about you: ‘Your end will be the doom and final date of truth and beauty.’
Sonnet 15

I consider how everything that grows stays perfect for only a little moment. This huge stage of the world presents nothing but shows, and the stars comment on them with their secret influence. I see that men grow like plants, cheered on and held back by the very same sky. They boast in their youthful sap, decline once they reach their height, and wear out their splendid state until no one remembers it. Then the thought of how briefly everything lasts sets you before my eyes, rich in youth. There, wasteful Time plots with Decay to change your youthful day into dirty night. And so, at war with Time for love of you, I graft new life onto you as fast as he takes it away.
Sonnet 16

But why don’t you make war in a stronger way on this bloody tyrant, Time? Why don’t you fortify yourself against your decay with a more blessed method than my barren rhymes? Now you stand at the peak of your happy hours. Many virgin gardens, not yet planted, would gladly bear you living flowers, much more like you than your painted portrait. That way the lines of life, your children, would renew your life. Neither Time’s paintbrush nor my amateur pen can make you live on in men’s eyes, either in your inner worth or your outward beauty. Giving yourself away keeps you alive. You must live on, drawn by your own sweet skill.
Sonnet 17

Who will believe my poetry in times to come if it is filled with your highest merits? Yet heaven knows my poetry is only like a tomb that hides your life and doesn’t show half your qualities. If I could describe the beauty of your eyes and list all your graces in fresh verses, future ages would say, ‘This poet lies. Such heavenly touches never touched human faces.’ So my pages, yellow with age, would be scorned like old men who talk more than they tell the truth. What you truly deserve would be called a poet’s frenzy, the overstretched meter of an old song. But if some child of yours were alive at that time, you would live twice—in the child, and in my rhyme.

chapters.title: Sonnets 18–40
paragraphs: Sonnet 18

Shall I compare you to a summer’s day? You are more lovely and more even-tempered. Rough winds shake the darling buds of May, and summer’s lease runs out far too soon. Sometimes the eye of heaven, the sun, shines too hot. Often his golden face is dimmed by clouds. And every beautiful thing loses its beauty sometime, stripped of its finery by chance or by nature’s changing course. But your eternal summer will not fade. You will not lose the beauty you own. Death will not brag that you wander in his shadow, because you will grow with time in these eternal lines. As long as men can breathe or eyes can see, this poem will live, and it will give life to you.
Sonnet 19

Devouring Time, blunt the lion’s paws, and make the earth devour her own sweet children. Pluck the sharp teeth from the fierce tiger’s jaws, and burn the long-lived phoenix alive in her own blood. Make happy and sad seasons as you speed by. Do whatever you want, swift-footed Time, to the wide world and all its fading sweet things. But I forbid you one most hateful crime. Oh, don’t carve my love’s beautiful forehead with your hours. Don’t draw any lines there with your ancient pen. Let him pass through your course untouched, as the model of beauty for the men who come after. Still, do your worst, old Time. Despite the harm you do, my love will live forever young in my poetry.
Sonnet 20

You have a woman’s face, painted by Nature’s own hand, you who are both master and mistress of my passion. You have a woman’s gentle heart, but it doesn’t know the fickle changes that are the habit of false women. Your eye is brighter than theirs and less false in its glances, and it turns to gold whatever it looks at. You are a man in looks, with all other looks under your control. You steal men’s eyes and amaze women’s souls. You were first created to be a woman. Then Nature, while she was making you, fell in love with you herself. By adding something, she cheated me out of you. She added one thing that is no use to my purpose. But since she picked you out and gave you a prick for women’s pleasure, let your love be mine, and let the use of your love be their treasure.
Sonnet 21

It isn’t the same with me as with that other poet whose Muse is stirred to verse by a painted, made-up beauty. He uses heaven itself as decoration and compares every beautiful thing to his beauty. He pairs his beloved in proud comparisons with the sun and the moon, with the earth and the sea’s rich gems, with April’s first flowers and every rare thing that heaven’s air encloses in this huge round world. Oh, let me, being true in love, just write truly. And then believe me, my love is as beautiful as any mother’s child, though not as bright as those golden candles, the stars, fixed in heaven’s air. Let those who like empty talk say more. I won’t overpraise something I don’t intend to sell.
Sonnet 22

My mirror won’t persuade me that I am old as long as you and youth are the same age. But when I see time’s wrinkles in you, then I expect death to end my days. For all that beauty that covers you is only the fitting clothing of my heart, which lives in your breast, as yours lives in mine. How, then, can I be older than you are? So, my love, take as much care of yourself as I will take of myself, not for my own sake but for yours. I carry your heart, and I will guard it as carefully as a loving nurse keeps her baby from harm. Don’t expect to get your heart back when mine is killed. You gave me yours never to be given back again.
Sonnet 23

I am like a nervous actor on the stage who forgets his part because of stage fright. Or I am like some fierce creature filled with too much rage, whose excess of strength weakens its own heart. In the same way, I don’t trust myself, and out of fear I forget to say the perfect words of love’s ritual. My love seems to weaken under its own strength, overloaded by the weight of my love’s power. Oh, then let my looks be my eloquence. Let them be the silent messengers of what my heart would say. They plead for love and hope for a reward, more than a tongue that has said more, more often. Oh, learn to read what silent love has written. To hear with the eyes is part of love’s fine intelligence.
Sonnet 24

My eye has played the painter and has fixed the image of your beauty on the canvas of my heart. My body is the frame that holds it. And seeing it in perspective is the finest art of a painter. You must look through the painter to see his skill and find where your true image is pictured. It is still hanging in the shop of my chest, and your eyes are the glass in its windows. Now see what good turns our eyes have done for each other. My eyes have drawn your shape, and yours are windows into my chest for me. The sun loves to peep through them to gaze at you inside. Yet eyes lack one skill to perfect their art. They draw only what they see; they don’t know the heart.
Sonnet 25

Let those whose stars are kind to them boast of public honors and proud titles. Fortune bars me from such triumphs. Instead, I quietly find unexpected joy in what I honor most. The favorites of great princes spread their lovely petals only like the marigold in the sun’s gaze. Their pride lies buried inside them, because at one frown from their prince they die in all their glory. The hardworking warrior, famous for fighting, is defeated once after a thousand victories. Then he is completely erased from the book of honor, and everything else he struggled for is forgotten. So I am happy, since I love and am loved where I can’t leave and can’t be thrown out.
Sonnet 26

Lord of my love, your worth has bound my duty to you tightly, as a servant to his master. I send you this written message to show my duty, not to show off my cleverness. My duty is so great that a wit as poor as mine may make it look bare, lacking the words to express it. But I hope some kind thought of yours will take it, naked as it is, into your soul. I hope so until whatever star guides my life shines on me with a favorable aspect. Then it will dress my ragged love in fine clothes and make me seem worthy of your sweet regard. Then I may dare to boast how much I love you. Until then, I won’t show my face where you might put me to the test.
Sonnet 27

Worn out with work, I hurry to my bed, the welcome rest for limbs tired from traveling. But then a journey starts inside my head, and it puts my mind to work once my body’s work is done. From far away, where I am staying, my thoughts set out on an eager pilgrimage to you. They keep my heavy eyelids wide open, staring into the same darkness the blind see. Except that my soul’s imagination shows your image to my unseeing eyes. Like a jewel hung in the ghostly night, it makes the black night beautiful and makes her old face look new. So you see, my limbs by day and my mind by night find no peace, because of you and because of me.
Sonnet 28

How can I come back in a happy state when I am shut out from the benefit of rest? Day’s burden is not eased by night. Instead, day is oppressed by night and night by day. Though the two are enemies, each ruling against the other, they shake hands and agree to torture me. Day does it with hard work, and night does it by making me grieve over how far I work, always farther away from you. To please the day, I tell him you are bright and that you lend him beauty when clouds blot out the sky. In the same way, I flatter the dark-skinned night. I tell her that when the sparkling stars do not twinkle, you light up the evening like gold. But every day the day drags my sorrows out longer, and every night the night makes my long grief feel stronger.
Sonnet 29

Sometimes I am out of luck and out of favor with people. Then I sit all alone and cry over my state as an outcast. I bother deaf heaven with my useless cries, look at myself, and curse my fate. I wish I were like someone with better prospects. I wish I had one man’s good looks and another man’s many friends. I want this man’s talent and that man’s range, and I am least satisfied with what I enjoy most. Yet while I almost hate myself for these thoughts, I happen to think of you. Then my mood is like the lark that rises at dawn from the gloomy earth and sings hymns at heaven’s gate. Remembering your sweet love brings me such riches that I would refuse to trade places with kings.
Sonnet 30

When I call up memories of the past to the court sessions of my sweet, silent thoughts, I sigh over the many things I wanted and never got. My old sorrows make me cry again over the precious time I have wasted. Then my eyes, which are not used to crying, can flood with tears for dear friends hidden in death’s endless night. I weep all over again for love’s pains that ended long ago. I moan over the cost of many sights now gone. Then I can grieve over grievances already finished. Sadly, I go from one sorrow to the next and count again the sad account of sorrows I have already mourned. I pay it again as if I had never paid it before. But if, while I am doing this, I think of you, dear friend, all my losses are restored and my sorrows end.
Sonnet 31

Your heart is made more precious because it holds all the hearts I had lost and believed were dead. Love reigns there, with all of love’s loving qualities, along with all the friends I thought were buried. Devoted love has stolen so many holy tears from my eyes at their funerals, paying what was owed to the dead. Now it turns out they were only moved away, and they lie hidden in you! You are the grave where buried love still lives. You are hung with the trophies of my lost loves. They gave you every share they had in me, so what many were owed now belongs to you alone. I see in you the faces of all the people I loved. And you, who are all of them, have all of me.
Sonnet 32

You may outlive the day when I die content, when that brute Death covers my bones with dust. If by chance you read these poor, rough lines by your dead lover once more, compare them with the better writing of later times. Even if every other writer’s pen outdoes them, keep them for the love in them, not for their rhymes, which happier poets will surpass. Then please grant me just this loving thought: ‘If my friend’s poetry had grown along with this improving age, his love would have produced something more precious than this. It would march alongside better-equipped poems. But since he died and other poets are better, I’ll read theirs for their style and his for his love.’
Sonnet 33

I have seen many a glorious morning flatter the mountain tops with its royal gaze. The sun kisses the green meadows with its golden face and turns pale streams to gold with heavenly magic. Then, soon after, it lets the lowest, darkest clouds drift across its heavenly face in ugly streaks. It hides its face from the lonely world and slips away to the west, unseen, in this disgrace. In just the same way, my own sun shone one early morning on my face in all its triumphant glory. But, alas, he was mine for only an hour. The clouds up above have hidden him from me now. Still, my love does not look down on him at all for this. Suns on earth may be stained when the sun in heaven is stained.
Sonnet 34

Why did you promise such a beautiful day and make me set out without my cloak? Why let low clouds catch up with me on my way and hide your splendor in their foul smoke? It is not enough for you to break through the cloud and dry the rain on my storm-beaten face. No one can praise a cure that heals the wound but does not erase the disgrace. Your shame cannot cure my grief either. Though you are sorry, I still suffer the loss. The wrongdoer’s sorrow gives only weak relief to the one who carries the heavy cross of the wrong. Ah, but the tears your love sheds are pearls. They are precious, and they pay the ransom for all your bad deeds.
Sonnet 35

Do not grieve anymore over what you have done. Roses have thorns, and silver fountains have mud. Clouds and eclipses stain both moon and sun, and the disgusting cankerworm lives in the sweetest bud. Everyone makes mistakes, and so do I right here. I justify your wrong by comparing it to these things. I corrupt myself by making excuses for your misdeeds. I make excuses for your sins that are bigger than the sins themselves. I bring reason to defend your sensual fault. The man you wronged has become your lawyer, and I start a lawful case against myself. Such a civil war goes on between my love and my hate that I cannot help becoming an accomplice to the sweet thief who cruelly robs me.
Sonnet 36

Let me admit that the two of us must be separate, even though our love is one and undivided. That way, the stains that stay on me will be carried by me alone, without your help. Our two loves share one regard for each other. But in our lives there is a spiteful thing that keeps us apart. It does not change love’s single power, yet it steals sweet hours from love’s pleasure. I may never again openly acknowledge you, in case my sorry guilt brings you shame. And you must not honor me with public kindness, unless you take that honor away from your own name. But don’t do that. I love you in such a way that, since you are mine, your good name is mine too.
Sonnet 37

An old, frail father takes delight in watching his lively child do youthful things. In the same way, I have been crippled by Fortune’s cruelest spite, and I take all my comfort from your worth and loyalty. Perhaps beauty, high birth, wealth or wit sits crowned among your qualities. Perhaps any one of these, or all of them, or more does. Whatever it is, I graft my love onto this rich store. Then I am not lame, poor or despised. This mere shadow of my love gives me such real substance that I am satisfied by your abundance. I live on a share of all your glory. Whatever is best, I wish that best for you. I have this wish, so I am ten times happy!
Sonnet 38

How can my Muse lack something to write about while you are alive and breathing? You pour your own sweet theme into my verse, and it is too excellent for any common paper to repeat. Oh, give yourself the thanks if anything I write is worth reading when you look at it. Who is so dull that he cannot write to you, when you yourself light up his imagination? Be the tenth Muse, ten times more worthy than the old nine that rhymers call on. And let whoever calls on you produce lasting verses that will outlive the distant future. If my small Muse pleases these picky times, let the labor be mine, but the praise yours.
Sonnet 39

Oh, how can I sing your worth modestly, when you are the whole better part of me? What can praising myself do for me? And what am I doing but praising myself when I praise you? For this very reason, let us live apart. Let our dear love lose the name of being one single thing. By being separated, I can give you the praise that you alone deserve. Oh, absence, what torture you would be! But your bitter free time gives me sweet permission to pass the hours thinking about love. Those thoughts sweetly beguile both time and my worries. And absence teaches me how to make one into two, by praising here the one who stays far away.
Sonnet 40

Take all my loves, my love, yes, take them all. What do you have then that you did not have before? You have no love, my love, that you could call true love. All my love was yours before you took this extra one. So if you take my lover because of your love for me, I cannot blame you for making use of her. But you should be blamed if you fool yourself by willfully tasting what you would otherwise refuse. I forgive your robbery, gentle thief, even though you steal the little I have. And yet love knows it is a greater grief to suffer a wrong from love than the open injury of hate. You lustful charmer, in whom even wickedness looks good, kill me with your cruelties, yet we must not be enemies.

chapters.title: Sonnets 41–60
paragraphs: Sonnet 41

Those pretty wrongs your freedom commits when I am sometimes absent from your heart suit your beauty and your age very well. Temptation always follows wherever you are. You are kind, and so you can be won. You are beautiful, and so you will be pursued. And when a woman woos, what woman’s son will coldly leave her before he has had his way? Oh dear! But you could still have kept away from my place. You could have scolded your beauty and your wandering youth, which lead you in their wild behavior even to a place where you are forced to break two promises. You break hers, because your beauty tempts her to you. You break yours, because your beauty makes you unfaithful to me.
Sonnet 42

That you have her is not my whole grief, although it could be said I loved her dearly. That she has you is the main thing I cry about. That loss in love hurts me more deeply. You loving offenders, this is how I will excuse you. You love her because you know I love her. And for my sake, she treats me badly in the same way, letting my friend test her out for my sake. If I lose you, my loss is my mistress’s gain. And if I lose her, my friend has found what I lost. They both find each other, and I lose both of them. And they both lay this cross on me for my sake. But here is the joy: my friend and I are one. What sweet flattery! Then she loves only me.
Sonnet 43

When my eyes are most tightly shut, they see best. All day long they look at things not worth noticing. But when I sleep, they look at you in dreams. Shining in the dark, they are aimed brightly through the dark. Your mere shadow makes shadows bright. So how lovely the real form of that shadow would look in clear daylight, with your much clearer light, when even your shadow shines like this to eyes that cannot see! How blessed, I say, my eyes would be to look at you in the living day, when in the dead of night your lovely, imperfect image stays on my sightless eyes through heavy sleep! Every day is as dark as night until I see you, and every night is bright as day when dreams show you to me.
Sonnet 44

If my dull, heavy flesh were made of thought, cruel distance would not block my way. In spite of space, I would be carried from the most remote places to where you stay. Then it would not matter if my foot stood on the land farthest away from you. Quick thought can jump over both sea and land as fast as it can think of the place it wants to be. But, ah, it kills me to think that I am not thought. I cannot leap across long stretches of miles when you are gone. Instead, since I am made of so much earth and water, I must wait on time’s slow schedule with my moaning. From such slow elements I get nothing but heavy tears, the signs of grief of both earth and water.
Sonnet 45

The other two elements, light air and cleansing fire, are both with you, wherever I am. The first is my thought, the second my desire, and they glide back and forth, here and gone, with quick motion. When these faster elements have gone off to you on a tender mission of love, my life, which is made of four elements, is left with only two. It sinks down toward death, weighed down with sadness. That lasts until my life’s balance is restored by those swift messengers coming back from you. Even now they have returned, assured of your good health, and they tell me about it. Hearing this, I am happy. But then, no longer glad, I send them back to you again and immediately grow sad.
Sonnet 46

My eye and my heart are fighting a war to the death over how to split the prize of seeing you. My eye wants to stop my heart from seeing your picture. My heart wants to deny my eye the free use of that right. My heart argues that you live inside him, in a private room that clear eyes can never see into. But the defendant denies that claim and says your lovely appearance lies inside him. To settle this claim, a jury of thoughts is sworn in, all of them tenants of the heart. Their verdict decides the clear eye’s share and the dear heart’s portion. It goes like this. My eye is owed your outward appearance, and my heart has the right to your heart’s inward love.
Sonnet 47

My eye and my heart have made a treaty, and now each does favors for the other. When my eye is starving for a look at you, or my heart, in love, is smothering itself with sighs, my eye feasts on my love’s picture. Then it invites my heart to the painted banquet. At other times my eye is my heart’s guest and shares in his loving thoughts. So, either through your picture or through my love, you are always present with me, even when you are away. You cannot move farther away than my thoughts can go. I am always with them, and they are always with you. Or, if they are asleep, your picture in front of my eyes wakes my heart, to the delight of both heart and eye.
Sonnet 48

How careful I was, when I set out on my journey, to lock every small thing behind the strongest bars. I wanted them kept unused for my own use, safe from thieving hands in secure places of trust! But you, compared to whom my jewels are trinkets, are my most precious comfort and now my greatest grief. You, the best of everything dear to me and my only concern, are left open to every common thief. I have not locked you up in any chest, except where you are not, though I feel you are there. That is inside the gentle enclosure of my chest, from which you can come and go as you please. And even from there, I fear, you will be stolen. Even honesty turns thief for a prize so precious.
Sonnet 49

I am preparing for that time, if it ever comes, when I see you frown at my faults. I mean the time when your love has totaled up its final sum, called to that audit by careful reasons. I am preparing for the time when you will walk past me like a stranger and barely greet me with that sun, your eye. That will be when love, changed from what it was, finds solemn reasons to stay cold. For that time, I shelter myself here in the knowledge of what little I deserve. I raise this hand of mine against myself to defend the lawful reasons on your side. You have the full strength of the law to leave poor me, since I can offer no reason why you should love me.
Sonnet 50

How heavily I travel on my way, when the end of my tiring trip, the thing I am heading for, only teaches comfort and rest to say: ‘This is how many miles you have come from your friend!’ The horse that carries me is tired with my sorrow. He plods dully on, carrying that weight in me, as if the poor creature somehow knew by instinct that his rider did not like speed, since it took him away from you. The bloody spur that I sometimes angrily drive into his hide cannot push him on. He answers it heavily with a groan that hurts me more sharply than the spur hurts his side. That same groan reminds me of this: my grief lies ahead of me, and my joy lies behind.
Sonnet 51

This is how my love can excuse the slow offense of my dull horse when I ride away from you. Why should I hurry away from where you are? Until I return, there is no need to rush. Oh, but what excuse will my poor animal find then, when even the greatest speed will seem slow? Then I would spur him on even if I were riding the wind. Even flying at full speed, I would feel no motion. Then no horse can keep up with my desire. Therefore desire, which is made of the most perfect love, will not neigh like dull flesh in his fiery race. Instead, love, for love’s sake, will excuse my old nag like this: ‘Since he went slowly on purpose when leaving you, I’ll run toward you and let him walk.’
Sonnet 52

I’m like the rich man whose blessed key can bring him to his sweet, locked-up treasure. He won’t look at it every hour, because that would blunt the fine edge of a pleasure he enjoys only seldom. That’s why feast days are so solemn and so rare. Since they come so seldom in the long year, they’re spaced out thinly, like precious stones, or like the chief jewels set in a necklace. In the same way, the time that keeps you from me is like my treasure chest. Or it’s like the wardrobe that hides a fine robe, ready to make some special moment especially blessed by unfolding its imprisoned splendor anew. You are blessed, because your worth gives room for triumph when I have you, and for hope when I lack you.
Sonnet 53

What are you made of, what is your substance, that millions of strange shadows and images wait on you? Everyone has only one shadow, each his own. Yet you, who are only one person, can lend your shadow to every image. Describe Adonis, and the portrait is only a poor imitation of you. Put every art of beauty onto Helen’s cheek, and you appear painted anew in Greek clothing. Speak of the spring and of the harvest’s plenty. The spring shows only a shadow of your beauty, and the harvest looks like your generosity. We recognize you in every blessed shape we know. You have some share in every outward grace. But for a faithful heart, you are like no one, and no one is like you.
Sonnet 54

Oh, how much more beautiful beauty seems when it has the sweet ornament that truth gives it! The rose looks lovely, but we think it lovelier for the sweet scent that lives inside it. The wild dog roses have color every bit as deep as the perfumed dye of real roses. They hang on the same kind of thorns and play just as playfully when the summer breeze opens their hidden buds. But since their only virtue is their looks, they live unwooed and fade unregarded. They die alone, for nobody. Sweet roses don’t do that. From their sweet deaths the sweetest perfumes are made. And it’s the same with you, beautiful and lovely young man. When your beauty fades, my verse will distill your truth and keep it.
Sonnet 55

Neither marble nor the gilded monuments of princes will outlive this powerful poem. You will shine more brightly in these lines than in a neglected stone, smeared with dirt by sluttish time. When destructive war knocks over statues, and riots tear up the work of masons, neither Mars’s sword nor war’s quick fire will burn this living record of your memory. You will stride forward against death and against the enmity that makes everything forgotten. Praise of you will always find room, even in the eyes of all the generations to come, who will wear this world out until Judgment Day. So, until the Judgment when you yourself rise again, you live in this poem and dwell in lovers’ eyes.
Sonnet 56

Sweet love, renew your strength. Don’t let anyone say that your edge is blunter than appetite. Appetite is satisfied today by eating, but tomorrow it’s sharpened back to its old strength. Love, be like that. Today you may fill your hungry eyes until they close, full to bursting. But tomorrow look again, and don’t kill the spirit of love with a dullness that never ends. Let this sad interval be like the ocean that divides two shores. Newly engaged lovers come to the banks every day, so that when they see love return, the sight is all the more blessed. Or call this interval winter, which is so full of hardship that it makes summer’s arrival three times more longed for and more precious.
Sonnet 57

Since I’m your slave, what should I do but wait on the hours and times when you want me? I have no precious time of my own to spend, and no duties to do until you require them. I don’t dare scold the endless hour while I, my sovereign, watch the clock for you. Nor do I dare think the bitterness of your absence is sour once you have said goodbye to your servant. I don’t dare ask with my jealous thoughts where you might be, or guess at what you’re doing. Instead, like a sad slave, I stay and think of nothing except how happy you make the people wherever you are. Love is such a complete fool that whatever you do with your will, it thinks no harm of it.
Sonnet 58

May the god who first made me your slave forbid that I should even think of controlling when you take your pleasure. May he forbid that I demand an account of your hours from you, since I’m your servant, bound to wait until you’re free! Oh, let me suffer, ready to come at your call, the prison of absence that your freedom brings me. Let my patience, tamed to endure, put up with every rebuke without accusing you of wronging me. Go wherever you like. Your privilege is so strong that you yourself may decide how to spend your time on whatever you want. It belongs to you alone to pardon yourself for crimes you commit against yourself. My job is to wait, even if waiting like this is hell, and not to blame your pleasure, whether it’s bad or good.
Sonnet 59

If there’s nothing new, and everything that exists has existed before, then how our brains are fooled! We labor to invent something, but we miscarry and give birth a second time to a child already born. Oh, if only history could look backward even five hundred years and show me your image in some old book, written since thought was first put into letters! Then I could see what the ancient world would say about this wonderful composition, your body. I could see whether we have improved, or whether they were better, or whether the cycle of time brings everything back the same. Oh, I’m sure that the clever writers of the past gave their admiring praise to worse subjects than you.
Sonnet 60

Just as the waves move toward the pebbly shore, our minutes hurry to their end. Each one changes place with the one ahead of it, and they all struggle forward, toiling in sequence. A newborn, once it enters the wide ocean of light, crawls toward maturity. Once it is crowned with maturity, evil eclipses fight against its glory, and Time, which gave the gift, now destroys it. Time pierces through the bloom set on youth and digs parallel furrows in beauty’s forehead. It feeds on the rarest things nature has made, and nothing exists except for his scythe to mow down. And yet my verse will stand into future times, praising your worth in spite of his cruel hand.

chapters.title: Sonnets 61–80
paragraphs: Sonnet 61

Is it your will that your image should keep my heavy eyelids open through the weary night? Do you want my sleep to be broken while shadows that look like you mock my eyes? Is it your spirit that you send so far from home to pry into what I do? Is it looking for shameful things and idle hours in me, which are the whole aim and purpose of your jealousy? Oh, no! Your love, though it’s great, isn’t that great. It’s my love that keeps my eyes awake. It’s my own true love that defeats my rest and makes me play the night watchman for your sake. I keep watch for you while you are awake somewhere else, far away from me and all too close to others.
Sonnet 62

The sin of self-love possesses my eyes completely, and all my soul, and every part of me. There’s no cure for this sin, because it’s rooted so deep in my heart. I think no face is as handsome as mine, no shape so perfect, no integrity worth as much. I judge my own worth so highly that I think I outdo everyone else in every kind of merit. But when my mirror shows me as I really am, battered and cracked by tanned old age, I read my self-love the opposite way. To love a self like that would be wicked. It’s you, my other self, whom I praise when I praise myself. I paint my old age with the beauty of your youthful days.
Sonnet 63

My love will someday be as I am now, crushed and worn out by Time’s harmful hand. The hours will drain his blood and fill his forehead with lines and wrinkles. His youthful morning will have traveled on to the steep night of old age. All the beauties he is now king of will be vanishing, or already gone from sight, stealing away the treasure of his springtime. Against that time I am building defenses now, against the cruel knife of destroying age. That way, age will never cut my sweet love’s beauty from memory, even though it cuts off my lover’s life. His beauty will be seen in these black lines of ink. They will live, and he will stay forever young in them.
Sonnet 64

I have seen Time’s cruel hand deface the rich and proud splendor of ages long dead and buried. I’ve seen once-lofty towers torn down, and everlasting brass made a slave to death’s rage. I have seen the hungry ocean gain ground on the kingdom of the shore. I’ve seen the solid land win territory from the sea, so each one’s gain is the other’s loss, and each one’s loss the other’s gain. I have seen such exchanges of condition, or greatness itself crumbling into decay. Ruin has taught me to think this through: Time will come and take my love away. This thought is like a death. It can do nothing but weep to have what it fears to lose.
Sonnet 65

Brass, stone, earth and the boundless sea all have their power overruled by sad mortality. So how can beauty win its case against this fury, when its strength is no greater than a flower’s? Oh, how can summer’s honey-sweet breath hold out against the destructive siege of the pounding days? Rocks that can’t be stormed are not strong enough, and gates of steel are not so strong that Time can’t wear them down. Oh, what a frightening thought! Where, alas, can Time’s best jewel be hidden from Time’s chest? What strong hand can hold back his swift foot? Who can stop him from plundering beauty? Oh, no one can. The only hope is this miracle: that my love may go on shining brightly in black ink.
Sonnet 66

Tired of all these things, I cry out for the rest of death. I’m tired of seeing merit born a beggar, and worthless nobodies dressed up in finery. I’m tired of seeing the purest faith sadly betrayed, and gilded honors shamefully handed to the wrong people. I’m tired of seeing virgin virtue roughly turned into a whore, and true perfection wrongly disgraced. I’m tired of seeing strength crippled by limping leadership, and art silenced by authority. I’m tired of seeing foolishness, dressed like a learned doctor, controlling real skill. I’m tired of plain truth being called stupidity, and good held captive, serving the captain Evil. Tired of all these things, I would like to leave them behind, except that if I die, I leave my love alone.
Sonnet 67

Ah, why should he live among such corruption and grace wickedness with his presence? Why should sin gain an advantage through him and adorn itself with his company? Why should false makeup imitate his cheek and steal a dead likeness of his living color? Why should poor imitation beauty go looking, indirectly, for painted roses, when his rose is real? Why should he live now that Nature is bankrupt, too poor in blood to blush through living veins? She has no treasury now except him. Though she boasts of many, she lives only on what he earns. Oh, she keeps him in store to show what wealth she had long ago, before these recent bad days.
Sonnet 68

So his cheek is a map of days gone by, when beauty lived and died the way flowers do now. That was before these false, bastard signs of beauty were born or dared to live on a living face. It was before the golden hair of the dead, which by right belonged to the grave, was cut off to live a second life on a second head. It was before a dead person’s fleece of hair was used to make someone else look fine. In him those holy, ancient times are seen, without any ornament, just itself and true. He makes no summer out of another’s greenery and robs nothing old to dress his beauty up as new. Nature keeps him as a map to show false Art what beauty was like long ago.
Sonnet 69

The parts of you that the world’s eye can see lack nothing that the heart’s thinking could improve. Every tongue, which is the voice of the soul, gives you that credit. They speak the bare truth, praising you the way even enemies would have to. So your outward appearance is crowned with outward praise. But the same tongues that give you what you’re owed change their tune and undo this praise by looking further than the eye can show. They look into the beauty of your mind, and they measure it, by guesswork, from your actions. Then their thoughts become rude, though their eyes were kind, and they add the rotten smell of weeds to your lovely flower. But the reason your scent doesn’t match your looks is this: you are growing common.
Sonnet 70

Being blamed won’t count as your flaw, since slander has always aimed at the beautiful. Suspicion is the ornament that comes with beauty, like a crow flying through heaven’s sweetest air. As long as you’re good, slander only proves your worth is greater, since the times are courting you. The cankerworm of vice loves the sweetest buds best, and you present a pure, unstained springtime of youth. You have passed through the ambush of your young days, either not attacked, or winning when you were. Yet this praise of yours can’t be enough to tie up envy, which is always set loose again. If some suspicion of evil did not cloud your appearance, you alone would own whole kingdoms of hearts.
Sonnet 71

Don’t mourn for me after I’m dead any longer than you hear the gloomy, sullen bell. It will announce to the world that I have fled from this vile world to live with the vilest worms. No, if you read this line, don’t remember the hand that wrote it. I love you so much that I would rather be forgotten in your sweet thoughts than have thinking of me make you sad. Oh, if, I say, you look at this poem when I am perhaps mixed into clay, don’t even repeat my poor name. Let your love decay along with my life. Otherwise, the wise world might look into your grief and mock you along with me after I’m gone.
Sonnet 72

Oh, the world might demand that you explain what merit I had that made you love me. So after my death, dear love, forget me completely, because you can prove nothing worthy in me. You couldn’t, unless you made up some kind, virtuous lie to do more for me than I deserve. You would have to hang more praise on dead me than stingy truth would willingly give. Oh, your true love might seem false in this, if out of love you speak well of me untruthfully. So let my name be buried where my body is, and live no longer, to shame neither me nor you. I am ashamed of what I produce, and so should you be, for loving things that are worth nothing.
Sonnet 73

In me you can see that time of year when a few yellow leaves, or none, hang on branches shaking against the cold. Those branches are like bare, ruined choir lofts where the sweet birds sang not long ago. In me you see the twilight of a day like the light that fades in the west after sunset. Little by little the black night takes it away, night that is death’s twin, sealing everything up in rest. In me you see the glow of a fire lying on the ashes of its youth. Those ashes are the deathbed where it must die, choked by the very fuel that once fed it. You see this, and it makes your love stronger, so that you love well what you must lose before long.
Sonnet 74

But be content. When that cruel arrest carries me off with no chance of bail, my life will still have some share in this poem. The poem will stay with you forever as a memorial. When you read this over, you read over the very part of me that was dedicated to you. The earth can only have earth, which is its due. My spirit, the better part of me, is yours. So you will have lost only the dregs of life, food for worms, when my body is dead. My body is the cowardly conquest of a wretch’s knife, too lowly for you to remember. The only worth of the body is what it contains, which is my spirit. And that spirit is this poem, and this poem stays with you.
Sonnet 75

You are to my thoughts what food is to life, or what sweet spring showers are to the ground. For the peace of having you, I struggle the way a miser struggles with his wealth. One moment I’m proud to own you, and the next I fear that this thieving age will steal my treasure. One moment I think it’s best to be alone with you. Then I think it would be even better for the world to see my pleasure. Sometimes I’m stuffed full from feasting on the sight of you, and soon after I’m completely starved for a look. I have or chase no pleasure except what I have from you, or what must be taken from you. So I starve and overeat day after day, either gorging on everything or having nothing at all.
Sonnet 76

Why is my poetry so empty of new decoration, so far from variety or quick changes of style? Why don’t I follow the fashion and glance aside at newly invented methods and strange new word compounds? Why do I always write the same way, always the same, and dress my creativity in such familiar clothes? Almost every word practically tells my name, showing where it was born and where it came from. Oh, know this, sweet love: I always write about you, and you and love are always my subject. So the best I can do is dress old words in new ways, spending again what has already been spent. Just as the sun is new and old every day, my love keeps telling what has already been told.
Sonnet 77

Your mirror will show you how your beauty is wearing away, and your sundial how your precious minutes are wasting. These blank pages will carry the imprint of your mind, and from this book you can learn this lesson. The wrinkles your mirror will truthfully show you will remind you of open-mouthed graves. By your sundial’s creeping shadow you can learn Time’s thieving progress toward eternity. Look! Whatever your memory can’t hold, write it down on these blank pages. You will find those thoughts, like children delivered from your brain and nursed, will introduce you to your own mind anew. These duties, as often as you look at them, will benefit you and greatly enrich your book.
Sonnet 78

I have called on you so often as my Muse, and found such good help in you for my poetry, that every other poet has copied my habit and now spreads their verse under your patronage. Your eyes, which taught the mute to sing loudly and heavy ignorance to fly high, have added feathers to the wings of the learned and given double majesty to those who already had grace. Yet be proudest of what I write, since its inspiration is yours and it is born of you. In other people’s works you only polish the style, and their skills are graced by your sweet graces. But you are all my art, and you lift my crude ignorance as high as learning itself.
Sonnet 79

While I alone called on you for help, my verse alone had all your gentle grace. But now my graceful lines have declined, and my sick Muse gives way to someone else. I admit, sweet love, that you as a lovely subject deserve the labor of a better pen. Yet whatever your poet invents about you, he steals from you and then pays it back to you. He lends you virtue, but he stole that word from your behavior. He gives you beauty, but he found it in your cheek. He can offer you no praise except what already lives in you. So don’t thank him for what he says, since you yourself pay what he owes you.
Sonnet 80

Oh, how I lose heart when I write about you, knowing that a better poet uses your name and spends all his strength praising it, which leaves me tongue-tied when I speak of your fame! But your worth is as wide as the ocean, and it carries the humble ship as well as the proudest sail. So my cheeky little boat, far inferior to his, boldly shows itself on your broad sea. The slightest help from you will keep me afloat, while he rides on your bottomless depths. Or, if I am wrecked, I am a worthless boat, and he is a tall, proud ship of fine build. So if he thrives and I am thrown away, the worst of it was this: my love was what destroyed me.

chapters.title: Sonnets 81–100
paragraphs: Sonnet 81

Either I will live to write your epitaph, or you will survive while I lie rotting in the earth. From now on, death cannot take your memory away, even though every part of me will be forgotten. Your name will have immortal life from these poems, though once I am gone I must die to the whole world. The earth can give me only an ordinary grave, while you will lie entombed in people’s eyes. Your monument will be my gentle verse, which eyes not yet created will read over and over. Tongues not yet born will repeat the story of your existence when everyone breathing now is dead. You will always live, such is the power of my pen, where breath is most alive: in the mouths of people.
Sonnet 82

I admit you were not married to my Muse, so you may, without dishonor, look over the dedications writers use for their beautiful subject, blessing every book. You are as fine in mind as you are in looks, and you find your worth goes beyond the limits of my praise. So you feel forced to look again for some fresher work stamped by these improving times. Do so, my love. Yet when they have invented whatever strained flourishes rhetoric can lend, you, who are truly beautiful, were truly portrayed in true plain words by your truth-telling friend. Their heavy makeup would be better used on cheeks that need color; on you it is wasted and abused.
Sonnet 83

I never saw that you needed makeup, so I never applied any paint to your beauty. I found, or thought I found, that you went far beyond the empty offering a poet owes. That is why I have been lazy in praising you. You yourself, alive and present, could well show how far a modern pen falls short when it speaks of worth, of the worth that grows in you. You blamed this silence on me as a sin, but being mute will be my greatest glory. By keeping quiet I do not damage beauty, while others, trying to give it life, bring it a tomb instead. There is more life in one of your beautiful eyes than both your poets can come up with in their praise.
Sonnet 84

Who can say the most, and who can say more than this rich praise: that you alone are you? Inside you is locked up the whole store of qualities that would be needed to produce your equal. Miserable poverty lives in a pen that does not lend some small glory to its subject. But whoever writes about you, if he can say that you are you, gives his story dignity by that alone. Let him just copy what is written in you, without spoiling what nature made so clear. Such a copy will make his talent famous and his style admired everywhere. But you add a curse to your beautiful blessings: you are fond of praise, which makes the praise of you worse.
Sonnet 85

My tongue-tied Muse politely keeps quiet, while praises of you, richly put together, are written down with a golden pen in precious phrases polished by all the Muses. I think good thoughts while others write good words. Like an illiterate parish clerk, I keep crying ‘Amen’ to every hymn that some able poet offers in the polished style of a refined pen. When I hear you praised, I say, ‘It’s so, it’s true,’ and add something more to the highest praise. But that is only in my thoughts, and my love for you holds first rank there, even if my words come last. So respect others for the breath of their words, and respect me for my silent thoughts, which speak in deeds.
Sonnet 86

Was it the proud, full sail of his great verse, setting out to win you, a prize far too precious, that buried my ripe thoughts inside my brain and made the womb they grew in into their tomb? Was it his spirit, taught by spirits to write higher than any mortal, that struck me dead? No. Neither he nor his companions, who help him at night, stunned my verse into silence. Neither he nor that friendly, familiar ghost who fools him every night with secret information can boast that they won by silencing me. I was not sick with any fear of them. But when your face filled up his lines, I had nothing left to write about, and that weakened mine.
Sonnet 87

Goodbye! You are too precious for me to own, and you probably know your own value. The rights your worth gives you set you free. My claims on you have all expired. How do I hold you except by your permission? And what have I done to deserve such riches? I lack any reason to receive this beautiful gift, so my right to it is going back to you. You gave yourself to me without knowing your own worth then, or else you were mistaken about me, the one you gave it to. So your great gift, which grew out of a misunderstanding, comes home again now that you judge better. So I have had you the way a flattering dream has you: asleep, I was a king, but awake, nothing of the kind.
Sonnet 88

When you are inclined to think little of me and hold my merit up to scorn, I will fight on your side against myself. I will prove you are virtuous even though you have broken your vows. I know my own weaknesses best, so I can tell a story in your support about hidden faults that disgrace me. That way, by losing me, you will win great glory. And I will gain by this too. Because all my loving thoughts are fixed on you, the injuries I do to myself help you and so help me twice over. My love is such, and I belong to you so completely, that I will bear every wrong myself to put you in the right.
Sonnet 89

Say that you left me because of some fault, and I will elaborate on that offense. Talk about my lameness, and I will limp at once, making no defense against your reasons. My love, you cannot disgrace me half as badly, to justify the change you want, as I will disgrace myself. Knowing what you want, I will kill our friendship and act like a stranger. I will stay away from the places you walk. Your sweet, beloved name will no longer live on my tongue, in case I, being too unworthy, should wrong it and perhaps reveal that we once knew each other. For your sake I will swear to argue against myself, because I must never love anyone you hate.
Sonnet 90

Then hate me whenever you like, and if ever, do it now. Now, while the world is set on thwarting everything I do, join the spite of fortune, make me bow, and don’t drop by later to add another loss. Ah, when my heart has escaped this sorrow, don’t come up at the rear of a grief already conquered. Don’t follow a windy night with a rainy morning, dragging out a defeat you have already planned. If you will leave me, don’t leave me last, after other petty griefs have done their damage. Come at the start, so that I taste the very worst of fortune’s power first. Then other kinds of grief that seem like grief now will not seem so, compared with losing you.
Sonnet 91

Some people take pride in their birth, some in their skill, some in their wealth, some in their physical strength. Some take pride in their clothes, even if they are ugly and newfangled. Some take pride in their hawks and hounds, some in their horses. Every temperament has its own matching pleasure, in which it finds a joy above all others. But these particular things are not my measure of happiness. I outdo them all with one overall best. Your love is better to me than high birth, richer than wealth, prouder than expensive clothes, and more delightful than hawks and horses. Having you, I can boast of everything people are proud of. I am wretched only in this: you could take all this away and make me the most wretched of all.
Sonnet 92

But do your worst to steal yourself away from me: for the rest of my life you are surely mine. My life will last no longer than your love, because it depends on that love of yours. So I don’t need to fear the worst wrongs, since my life will end with the least of them. I see that I am in a better position than one that depends on your moods. You cannot torment me with a changing mind, since my life would end the moment you turned against me. Oh, what a happy claim I find I have: happy to have your love, and happy to die! But what is so blessed and beautiful that it fears no stain? You may be unfaithful, and yet I would not know it.
Sonnet 93

So I will live on, assuming you are faithful, like a deceived husband. That way love’s face may still look like love to me, though it has newly changed. Your looks would be with me, but your heart somewhere else. Since no hatred can live in your eyes, I cannot tell from them that you have changed. In many people’s faces, the history of a false heart is written in moods, frowns and strange wrinkles. But heaven decided, when you were created, that sweet love should always live in your face. Whatever your thoughts or the workings of your heart might be, your looks would show nothing but sweetness. How much your beauty will grow to look like Eve’s apple if your sweet virtue does not match your appearance!
Sonnet 94

There are people who have the power to hurt and will not use it. They do not do the thing their looks suggest they will do. They move others but are themselves like stone: unmoved, cold and slow to be tempted. Such people rightly inherit heaven’s blessings and protect nature’s riches from being wasted. They are the lords and owners of their faces, while others are only servants managing their excellence. The summer’s flower is sweet to the summer, even if it lives and dies only for itself. But if that flower is infected with disease, the lowliest weed outshines its dignity. The sweetest things turn the sourest through their own actions: lilies that rot smell far worse than weeds.
Sonnet 95

How sweet and lovely you make the shame that spots the beauty of your budding reputation, like a cankerworm in a fragrant rose! Oh, in what sweetness you wrap up your sins! The tongue that tells the story of your days, making dirty comments about your love affairs, cannot criticize you except as a kind of praise. Just naming your name blesses a bad report. Oh, what a mansion those vices have, which chose you as their home! There, beauty’s veil covers every stain and turns everything eyes can see into something beautiful. Take care, dear heart, with this great license of yours. Even the hardest knife, used badly, loses its edge.
Sonnet 96

Some say your fault is youth, some say it’s lust. Some say your charm is youth and playful fun. Both your charm and your faults are loved by people high and low. You turn the faults that come to you into graces. Just as the cheapest jewel is highly valued on the finger of a queen on her throne, so the errors seen in you are translated into truths and taken for good things. How many lambs the cruel wolf could betray if he could change his looks into a lamb’s! How many admirers you could lead astray if you used the full power of your position! But don’t do that. I love you so much that, since you are mine, your good name is mine too.
Sonnet 97

How like winter my absence from you has been, you who are the pleasure of the passing year! What freezing cold I have felt, what dark days I have seen, what bareness of old December everywhere! And yet this time away was summertime. Fruitful autumn was swollen with a rich harvest, carrying the lusty load that spring had planted, like widows’ wombs pregnant after their husbands’ deaths. Yet this abundant offspring seemed to me nothing but the hope of orphans and fruit without a father. For summer and its pleasures wait on you, and with you away, even the birds are silent. Or, if they do sing, it is with such a gloomy mood that the leaves turn pale, fearing winter is near.
Sonnet 98

I have been away from you in the spring, when proud, many-colored April, dressed in all his finery, put a youthful spirit into everything, so that even gloomy Saturn laughed and leaped with him. Yet neither the songs of the birds nor the sweet smell of flowers of different scents and colors could make me tell any cheerful summer story. Nor could they make me pick the flowers from the proud earth where they grew. I did not marvel at the whiteness of the lily or praise the deep red of the rose. They were only sweet, only images of delight, drawn as copies of you, the model for them all. Yet with you away, it still seemed like winter, and I played with these flowers as if they were your shadow.
Sonnet 99

This is how I scolded the early violet: ‘Sweet thief, where did you steal your sweet scent from, if not from my love’s breath? The proud purple that lives on your soft cheek as its color, you have dyed too heavily in my love’s veins.’ I condemned the lily for stealing the whiteness of your hand, and the buds of marjoram had stolen your hair. The roses stood fearfully on their thorns, one blushing red with shame, another white with despair. A third, neither red nor white, had stolen from both, and had added your breath to its robbery. But for its theft, in the full pride of its growth, a vengeful cankerworm ate it up until it died. I noticed more flowers, but I could not see one that had not stolen its sweetness or its color from you.
Sonnet 100

Where are you, Muse, that you forget for so long to speak about the one who gives you all your power? Are you spending your passion on some worthless song, dimming your power to shed light on low subjects? Come back, forgetful Muse, and at once make up for the time you wasted so idly, in gentle verse. Sing to the ear that values your songs and gives your pen both skill and subject matter. Get up, lazy Muse, and examine my love’s sweet face to see if Time has carved any wrinkle there. If there is one, write a satire against decay, and make Time’s plunder despised everywhere. Give my love fame faster than Time wastes life. That way you will block his scythe and curved blade.

chapters.title: Sonnets 101–126
paragraphs: Sonnet 101

Oh, truant Muse, how will you make up for neglecting truth that is steeped in beauty? Both truth and beauty depend on my love, and so do you, and you are honored by it. Answer, Muse. Perhaps you will say, ‘Truth needs no added color, since its color is fixed. Beauty needs no paintbrush to set down beauty’s truth. The best is best if it is never mixed with anything.’ Because he needs no praise, will you be silent? Don’t excuse silence that way. It is in your power to make him long outlive a gilded tomb and be praised by ages yet to come. So do your job, Muse. I will teach you how to make him look, long from now, just as he looks today.
Sonnet 102

My love has grown stronger, though it seems weaker. I don’t love any less, even though I show it less. Love is turned into merchandise when its owner advertises its rich value everywhere. Our love was new, and still only in its spring, when I used to greet it with my songs. In the same way the nightingale sings at the start of summer and stops her music as the days grow riper. It isn’t that summer is less pleasant now than when her mournful hymns hushed the night. It is that wild music now weighs down every branch, and sweet things that become common lose their precious delight. So, like her, I sometimes hold my tongue, because I don’t want to bore you with my song.
Sonnet 103

Oh, what a poor thing my Muse produces! She has such a wide field in which to show off her glory, yet the subject on its own, bare and plain, is worth more than it is with my praise added to it. Oh, don’t blame me if I can’t write anymore! Look in your mirror, and a face appears there that completely outdoes my clumsy imagination. It makes my lines look dull and brings me shame. So wouldn’t it be a sin to try to improve the subject and only spoil what was already fine? My verses aim at nothing else but to describe your graces and your gifts. And your own mirror shows you more, much more, than my verse can hold whenever you look into it.
Sonnet 104

To me, my beautiful friend, you can never be old. Your beauty seems the same now as it was when I first laid eyes on your eyes. Three cold winters have shaken three proud summers’ leaves from the forests. In the passing of the seasons I have watched three beautiful springs turn to yellow autumn. I have seen three April perfumes burned up in three hot Junes since I first saw you fresh, and you are still young and green. Ah, but beauty is like the hand of a clock. It creeps away from its number, and no one sees it move. In the same way your sweet complexion, which I think is standing still, is actually moving, and my eye may be fooled. Because I fear that, hear this, you ages not yet born: before you were born, the summer of beauty was already dead.
Sonnet 105

Don’t let my love be called idol worship, and don’t let my beloved look like an idol. It’s true that all my songs and praises are alike. They are addressed to one person, about one person, always the same and always so. My love is kind today and kind tomorrow, always constant in a wonderful excellence. So my verse is limited to constancy. It expresses one thing and leaves out variety. ‘Fair, kind, and true’ is my whole subject. ‘Fair, kind, and true,’ put into other words. All my creativity is spent on varying this, three themes in one, which gives me wonderful room to work. Beauty, kindness, and truth have often lived separately. Until now, the three never lived together in one person.
Sonnet 106

When I read in the chronicles of times gone by the descriptions of the most beautiful people, I see beauty making old poems beautiful. Those poems praise dead ladies and lovely knights. Then, in their catalogs of the best features of sweet beauty—hand, foot, lip, eye and brow—I see that those old writers were trying to express exactly the kind of beauty you possess now. So all their praises are nothing but prophecies of our time, all of them picturing you in advance. And because they could only look at you with prophetic eyes, they didn’t have enough skill to sing your worth. As for us, who see these present days, we have eyes to marvel at you, but we lack the tongues to praise you.
Sonnet 107

Neither my own fears nor the prophetic soul of the wide world, dreaming about things to come, can set a limit on the lease of my true love. People assumed that lease would expire, doomed to end on a fixed date. The mortal moon has come through her eclipse, and the gloomy prophets laugh at their own predictions. Uncertain things are now crowned as certain, and peace announces olive branches that will last forever. Now, with the healing drops of this soothing season, my love looks fresh, and Death gives in to me. In spite of him, I will live on in this humble poem, while he lords it over dull tribes who have no words. And you will find your monument in this poem, when the crests of tyrants and their brass tombs have worn away.
Sonnet 108

What is there in the brain that ink can write down that I haven’t already used to show you my true spirit? What’s new to say, what’s left to record, that could express my love or your precious worth? Nothing, sweet boy. But still, like holy prayers, I must say the very same thing over each day. I count no old thing as old: you are mine, I am yours, just as when I first made your fair name holy. So eternal love, in love’s fresh form, doesn’t care about the dust and damage of age. It gives no room to wrinkles, even though they are inevitable. Instead it makes old age its servant forever. It finds the first idea of love born there again, where time and outward appearance would show it dead.
Sonnet 109

Oh, never say that I was unfaithful at heart, even though being away seemed to cool my flame. I could as easily leave myself as leave my soul, which lives in your chest. That is my home of love. If I have wandered, I come back again like a traveler. I return on time, not changed by the time away, so that I myself bring the water to wash away my stain. My nature may be ruled by all the weaknesses that attack every kind of person. But never believe it could be so absurdly corrupted that it would leave all your goodness for nothing. I call this whole wide universe nothing except you, my rose. In it, you are my everything.
Sonnet 110

Alas, it’s true, I have gone here and there and made myself a clown for everyone to look at. I have wounded my own thoughts, sold cheaply what is most precious, and committed old offenses with new loves. It’s very true that I have looked at faithfulness sideways and coldly. But, by heaven above, these swerves gave my heart a new youth. My worse experiments proved that you are my best love. Now all that is over, except what will never end. I will never again sharpen my appetite on some new trial just to test an older friend. You are a god of love, and I am bound to you. So welcome me, you who are next best to heaven, into your pure and most, most loving arms.
Sonnet 111

Oh, for my sake, scold Fortune, the goddess who is guilty of my harmful actions. She didn’t provide anything better for my life than a public living, which breeds public manners. That is why my name is branded with disgrace. And because of it my nature is almost overcome by what it works in, like the dyer’s hand. So pity me, and wish that I were made new. Meanwhile, like a willing patient, I will drink medicines of vinegar against my strong infection. I won’t think any bitterness bitter, and I won’t refuse a double penance to correct what needs correcting. So pity me, dear friend, and I promise you that your pity alone is enough to cure me.
Sonnet 112

Your love and pity fill in the scar that common scandal stamped on my forehead. Why should I care who speaks well or badly of me, as long as you cover my faults with green and approve of my good points? You are my whole world, and I must try to learn my shames and praises from your lips. No one else matters to me, and I matter to no one alive who could change my hardened feelings for right or wrong. I throw all concern for other people’s voices into such a deep pit that my ears are closed, like a deaf adder’s, to both critics and flatterers. Notice how I excuse my neglect of them. You are so firmly rooted in my mind that I think the rest of the world is dead.
Sonnet 113

Since I left you, my eye lives in my mind. The eye that guides me as I move around has given up part of its job and is partly blind. It seems to see, but in fact it is shut off. It delivers to my heart no image of any bird, flower, or shape that it catches. My mind has no share in the quick things the eye sees, and the eye itself doesn’t keep what it catches. Whether it sees the roughest or gentlest sight, the sweetest face or the most deformed creature, the mountain or the sea, the day or the night, the crow or the dove, it turns them all into your features. My mind can’t hold anything more, because it is full of you. So my most faithful mind makes my eye unfaithful.
Sonnet 114

Is it that my mind, crowned with you, drinks up flattery, the plague of kings? Or should I say that my eye tells the truth, and that your love taught it this alchemy? Maybe love taught it to turn monsters and shapeless things into angels that look like your sweet self. It turns every bad thing into a perfect best as fast as objects come into its gaze. Oh, it’s the first one: it’s flattery in my seeing, and my great mind drinks it up like a king. My eye knows very well what suits my mind’s taste, and it prepares the cup to please that palate. If the cup is poisoned, the sin is smaller, because my eye loves it and drinks first.
Sonnet 115

The lines I wrote before are lies, even the ones that said I couldn’t love you more. But back then my judgment didn’t know any reason why my fullest flame would later burn even brighter. I was thinking about Time and its millions of accidents. Time creeps in between promises and changes the decrees of kings. It tans sacred beauty, dulls the sharpest intentions, and turns strong minds toward the path of changing things. So, fearing Time’s tyranny, why couldn’t I say then, ‘Now I love you best’? I was certain beyond all uncertainty, crowning the present and doubting the rest. But love is a baby, so I couldn’t say that. It would mean calling full-grown something that is still growing.
Sonnet 116

Don’t let me admit that anything can stand in the way of the marriage of true minds. Love is not love if it changes when it finds a change in the beloved. It is not love if it bends and leaves when the other leaves. Oh, no! Love is a fixed landmark that looks at storms and is never shaken. It is the star that guides every wandering ship. Its value is beyond measure, even though sailors can measure its height. Love isn’t Time’s fool, even though rosy lips and cheeks fall within the sweep of his curved sickle.
