Love doesn’t change with Time’s brief hours and weeks. It lasts all the way to the edge of Judgment Day. If this is wrong and it’s proved against me, then I never wrote anything, and no man ever loved.
Sonnet 117

Go ahead and accuse me. Say that I have held back everything I should have given to repay your great merits. Say that I forgot to call on your precious love, though every bond ties me to it day after day. Say that I have spent a lot of time with strangers and given away to the moment what was rightfully yours, bought at a high price. Say that I have raised my sails to every wind that would carry me farthest out of your sight. Write down both my stubbornness and my mistakes. Add your suspicions to what you can prove. Bring me into the line of fire of your frown. But don’t shoot at me in newly awakened hatred. My defense is that I was only trying to test how constant and true your love is.
Sonnet 118

To sharpen our appetite, we stimulate our palate with spicy mixtures. To prevent illnesses we can’t yet see, we make ourselves sick with a purge to avoid getting sick. In just the same way, being full of your sweetness, which never grows sickening, I made bitter sauces my diet. Sick of feeling well, I found it somehow fitting to be ill before there was any real need. So this clever strategy in love, of heading off troubles that didn’t exist, turned into real faults. It brought a healthy state to need medicine. That state, overfull of goodness, tried to be cured by sickness. But I learn from this, and I find the lesson true: drugs poison anyone who fell sick of you that way.
Sonnet 119

What potions of Siren tears have I drunk, distilled in flasks as foul as hell inside? I set fears against hopes and hopes against fears, always losing just when I thought I was winning! What miserable mistakes my heart has made, while it thought it had never been so blessed! How my eyes have been jerked out of their sockets in the madness of this raging fever! Oh, the benefit of bad things! Now I find it true that what is good is made even better by evil. And love that was ruined, once it is rebuilt, grows more beautiful than at first, stronger and far greater. So I return, scolded, to what makes me happy, and through evil I gain three times more than I have spent.
Sonnet 120

The fact that you were once unkind to me helps me now. Because of the sorrow I felt then, I must bow down under my own wrongdoing, unless my nerves were made of brass or hammered steel. If you were as shaken by my unkindness as I was by yours, you have been through hell. And I, like a tyrant, haven’t taken the time to consider how much I once suffered from your offense. Oh, if only our night of sorrow had reminded me deep down how hard real grief hits! Then I would have quickly offered you, as you once offered me, the humble ointment that suits wounded hearts. But now your offense becomes a payment. My offense pays for yours, and yours must pay for mine.
Sonnet 121

It’s better to be wicked than to be thought wicked, when you are blamed for being wicked even though you aren’t. Then you even lose the honest pleasure, which is judged wicked not by how we feel but by how others see it. Why should other people’s false, corrupt eyes wink knowingly at my playful passions? Why should my weaknesses be spied on by people even weaker than me? In their minds they count as bad what I think is good. No, I am what I am. Those who aim at my offenses are only counting up their own. I may be straight even though they are crooked. My actions must not be judged by their foul thoughts. Unless they claim this general evil: that all men are bad and thrive in their badness.
Sonnet 122

Your gift, your notebook, is already in my brain, written out fully in lasting memory. It will last longer than that useless page, beyond any date, even to eternity. Or at least it will last as long as my brain and heart are able by nature to survive. Until each of them surrenders its part of you to total oblivion, your record can never be lost. That poor notebook couldn’t hold as much, and I don’t need tally sticks to count up your precious love. So I was bold enough to give the notebook away. I trust instead the tablets of memory, which hold more of you. To keep an aid to remember you would be to suggest that I am forgetful.
Sonnet 123

No, Time, you won’t boast that I change. Your pyramids, built up with new strength, are nothing new or strange to me. They are just new costumes on something seen before. Our lives are short, and so we admire the old things you pass off on us as new. We would rather believe they were made just for us than think we have heard of them before. I defy both you and your records. I am not amazed by the present or the past. Your records and what we see both lie, made bigger or smaller by your constant rushing. This I promise, and it will always be so: I will stay true in spite of your scythe and you.
Sonnet 124

If my precious love were only the child of circumstance, it might be disowned as Fortune’s bastard with no father. It would be subject to Time’s love or Time’s hate, a weed gathered with weeds or a flower gathered with flowers. No, it was built far away from chance. It doesn’t suffer in smiling splendor, and it doesn’t fall under the blow of oppressed discontent. Our times tempt people like us toward that kind of thing. My love doesn’t fear political scheming, that heretic, which only works on short-term leases of a few hours. Instead it stands alone, hugely wise, so that it neither grows with heat nor drowns with rain. I call as witnesses to this the fools of time, who die repenting after having lived for crime.
Sonnet 125

Would it mean anything to me if I carried the canopy over a great person, honoring outward show with my outward behavior? Or if I laid great foundations meant for eternity, which turn out to be shorter-lived than waste and ruin? Haven’t I seen people who care about appearance and favor lose everything and more by paying too high a rent? They gave up simple taste for fancy sweets, pitiful successes worn out by their staring. No, let me be devoted in your heart. And you, accept my offering, poor but freely given. It isn’t mixed with second-rate stuff and knows no trickery. It is only an exchange between us: myself for you. Get away, you bribed informer! A true soul, when it is most accused, is least in your power.
Sonnet 126

Oh you, my lovely boy, who hold in your power Time’s fickle hourglass, his fickle hour! You have grown by aging, and in doing so you show your lovers withering while your sweet self grows. Nature is the queen who rules over ruin. If she keeps pulling you back as you move forward, she keeps you for this reason: so that her skill may disgrace time and kill the miserable minutes. Still, fear her, you darling of her pleasure! She may hold on to her treasure for a while, but not forever. Her account, though delayed, must be paid. And her final settlement is to hand you over.

chapters.title: Sonnets 127–152: The Dark Lady
paragraphs: Sonnet 127

In the old days black was not considered beautiful. Or if it was, it wasn’t called beauty. But now black is beauty’s rightful heir, and beauty is slandered with the shame of being illegitimate. Ever since everyone’s hand has taken on Nature’s power, making the ugly look fair with the false, borrowed face of makeup, sweet beauty has no name and no holy shrine. It is treated as profane, if it doesn’t actually live in disgrace. That is why my mistress’s eyes are raven black. Her eyes are dressed to match, and they seem to be mourning. They mourn for those who weren’t born beautiful but don’t lack beauty, slandering creation with false value. Yet her eyes mourn so becomingly in their grief that everyone says beauty should look like that.
Sonnet 128

You are my music. When you play music on that blessed wood, it sounds as your sweet fingers move it, and you gently sway the harmony of wires that amazes my ears. How often, then, I envy those keys that leap so nimbly to kiss the soft inside of your hand! Meanwhile my poor lips, which should reap that harvest, stand by blushing at the wood’s boldness. To be touched like that, my lips would trade places with those dancing chips of wood. Your fingers walk over them with a gentle step, making dead wood more blessed than living lips. Since those cheeky keys are so happy with this, give them your fingers, and give me your lips to kiss.
Sonnet 129

Lust, once acted on, is a shameful waste of the spirit’s energy. And until it is acted on, lust is treacherous, murderous, bloody, full of guilt, savage, extreme, brutal, cruel and not to be trusted. No sooner is it enjoyed than it is instantly despised. It is chased beyond all reason, and no sooner is it had than it is hated beyond all reason, like a swallowed bait laid on purpose to drive whoever takes it mad. It is mad in pursuit and mad in possession too. Having had it, having it, and seeking to have it, it is always extreme. It is bliss while you are experiencing it, and once experienced, it is pure misery. Beforehand it is a joy you look forward to; afterward it is only a dream. The whole world knows all this well, yet nobody knows well enough to avoid the heaven that leads men to this hell.
Sonnet 130

My mistress’s eyes are nothing like the sun. Coral is far redder than her lips are. If snow is white, then her breasts are a dull grayish brown. If hair is wire, then black wires grow on her head. I have seen roses that are mingled red and white, but I see no roses like that in her cheeks. And some perfumes give more delight than the breath that stinks from my mistress. I love to hear her speak, yet I know very well that music has a far more pleasing sound. I admit I have never seen a goddess walk, but my mistress, when she walks, treads on the ground. And yet, by heaven, I think my love is as rare as any woman who has been misrepresented with false comparisons.
Sonnet 131

You are just as tyrannical, exactly as you are, as those women whose beauty makes them proud and cruel. You know very well that to my dear, doting heart you are the fairest and most precious jewel. Yet honestly, some people who look at you say that your face does not have the power to make a lover groan. I do not dare to be so bold as to say they are wrong, although I swear it to myself in private. And to prove that what I swear is not false, a thousand groans that come just from thinking about your face, one right after another, bear witness that your blackness is the fairest thing in my judgment. You are black in nothing except your deeds, and that, I think, is where this slander about your looks comes from.
Sonnet 132

I love your eyes, and they seem to pity me. Knowing that your heart torments me with scorn, they have dressed in black and become loving mourners, looking with pretty compassion on my pain. And truly, the morning sun in the sky does not suit the gray cheeks of the east any better than those two mourning eyes suit your face. Nor does the full evening star that brings on the night give even half that glory to the somber west. Oh, then let it suit your heart just as well to mourn for me, since mourning makes you so graceful, and let your pity dress every part of you alike. Then I will swear that Beauty herself is black, and that everyone who lacks your coloring is ugly.
Sonnet 133

Curse that heart of yours that makes my heart groan for the deep wound it gives both my friend and me! Isn’t it enough to torture me alone? Must my sweetest friend also be made a slave to slavery? Your cruel eye has taken me away from myself, and you have taken an even harder hold on my second self, my friend. So I am abandoned by him, by myself and by you. That is a torment three times threefold to suffer. Lock my heart up in the prison of your steel heart, but then let my poor heart bail out my friend’s heart. Whoever keeps me, let my heart be his guard. Then you cannot treat me harshly in my jail. And yet you will, because I, being locked inside you, am necessarily yours, along with everything in me.
Sonnet 134

So now I have confessed that he belongs to you, and that I myself am mortgaged to your desire. I will give up myself as forfeit, so long as you return that other self of mine to be my comfort forever. But you will not, and he does not want to be free, because you are greedy and he is kind. He only signed as my guarantor, co-signing for me under that same bond, which now binds him just as tightly. You will take everything your beauty legally entitles you to, you moneylender who puts everything out at interest. You will sue a friend who became a debtor only for my sake. So I lose him through my own unkind misuse of him. I have lost him; you have both him and me. He pays the whole debt, and yet I am still not free.
Sonnet 135

Whatever other woman has her wish, you have your ‘Will,’ and ‘Will’ besides, and ‘Will’ to spare. I, who keep pestering you, am more than enough, adding to your sweet will in this way. Will you, whose will is so large and roomy, not agree even once to hide my will in yours? Shall will in other men seem perfectly welcome, while my will finds no kind acceptance? The sea is all water, yet it still takes in rain and adds it to its abundant store. So you, being rich in ‘Will,’ should add to your ‘Will’ one will of mine, to make your large will larger. Do not let an unkind ‘No’ kill your honest suitors. Think of them all as one, and count me as part of that one ‘Will.’
Sonnet 136

If your soul scolds you for letting me come so close, swear to your blind soul that I was your ‘Will.’ And your soul knows that will, or desire, is allowed in there. So, sweet, fulfill my love-suit this far for love’s sake. ‘Will’ will fill the treasury of your love. Yes, fill it full of wills, and let my will be one of them. In things that hold a great deal, we easily find that one among a large number counts as none. So let me pass uncounted in the crowd, though in your inventory I must count as one. Consider me nothing, as long as it pleases you to hold that nothing, me, as something sweet to you. Just make my name your love, and keep loving it always. Then you will love me, because my name is ‘Will.’
Sonnet 137

You blind fool, Love, what are you doing to my eyes, so that they look and do not see what they see? They know what beauty is and see where it lies, yet they take the worst to be the best. My eyes have been corrupted by looking too fondly. They are anchored in the bay where all men ride at anchor. If so, why have you made hooks out of my eyes’ falseness, and tied my heart’s judgment to them? Why should my heart think that a private plot of land, when it knows that she is the whole world’s common field? Or why should my eyes, seeing this, say it is not so, putting fair truth on such a foul face? My heart and eyes have gone wrong about what is truly right, and now they have been handed over to this plague of falseness.
Sonnet 138

When my love swears that she is completely truthful, I believe her even though I know she is lying. I do it so that she might think I am some naive young man, inexperienced in the world’s false tricks. So I vainly imagine that she thinks I am young, although she knows my best days are behind me. I simply pretend to believe her lying tongue. In this way, the plain truth is hidden on both sides. But why doesn’t she say that she is unfaithful? And why don’t I say that I am old? Oh, love’s best clothing is the appearance of trust, and an older person in love does not like to have his years counted. So I lie with her, and she lies with me, and by our lies we flatter each other about our faults.
Sonnet 139

Oh, do not ask me to justify the wrong that your unkindness does to my heart. Do not wound me with your eye, but with your tongue. Use your power openly and directly, and do not kill me with tricks. Tell me you love someone else, but when I am in sight, dear heart, do not glance your eye away from me. Why do you need to wound me with cunning, when your strength is already more than my overwhelmed defenses can withstand? Let me make excuses for you. Ah, my love knows well that her pretty looks have been my enemies. So she turns those enemies away from my face, so that they can shoot their injuries somewhere else. Yet do not do that. Since I am already nearly killed, finish me off with your looks and put an end to my pain.
Sonnet 140

Be as wise as you are cruel. Do not push my silent patience with too much scorn. Otherwise sorrow may give me words, and those words may describe what my pain is like, a pain that no one pities. If I could teach you some sense, it would be better for you, even if you do not love me, to at least tell me that you do. In the same way, irritable sick men near death hear nothing from their doctors except news that they are getting well. For if I were to despair, I would go mad, and in my madness I might speak badly of you. This world, which twists everything to the worst, has now grown so bad that mad listeners believe mad slanderers. So that I do not become one, and you are not slandered, keep your eyes looking straight at me, even if your proud heart wanders far away.
Sonnet 141

Honestly, I do not love you with my eyes, because they notice a thousand faults in you. It is my heart that loves what they despise, and it is happy to dote on you in spite of what they see. My ears are not delighted by the sound of your voice either. Neither my sensitive touch, which is easily drawn to low pleasures, nor my taste, nor my smell wants to be invited to any feast of the senses alone with you. But neither my five mental faculties nor my five senses can talk one foolish heart out of serving you. My heart leaves me ungoverned, just the shell of a man, so that it can be the slave and wretched servant of your proud heart. The only gain I count from my affliction is this: the woman who makes me sin also gives me my punishment.
Sonnet 142

Love is my sin, and your precious virtue is hate, a hatred of my sin, which is based on sinful loving. But oh, just compare your own situation with mine, and you will find that mine does not deserve blame. Or if it does, it should not come from those lips of yours. They have defiled their scarlet beauty and sealed false contracts of love as often as mine have. They have robbed other women’s marriage beds of what was owed to them. Let it be lawful for me to love you, just as you love those men whom your eyes court, the way my eyes beg you. Plant pity in your heart, so that when it grows, your pity may deserve to be pitied in return. If you try to get what you yourself withhold, may you be refused by your own example!
Sonnet 143

Look how a careful housewife runs to catch one of her chickens that has broken loose. She sets down her baby and hurries off at full speed to chase the thing she wants to keep. Meanwhile her neglected child chases after her and cries to catch her, while her busy attention is fixed on following what flees in front of her. She pays no attention to her poor baby’s distress. In the same way, you run after what flies away from you, while I, your baby, chase you from far behind. But if you catch what you are hoping for, turn back to me. Play the mother’s part: kiss me and be kind. Then I will pray that you may have your ‘Will,’ if you turn back and quiet my loud crying.
Sonnet 144

I have two loves, one bringing comfort and the other despair, and like two spirits they keep tempting me. The better angel is a very fair man. The worse spirit is a woman with a dark coloring. To win me quickly to hell, my female evil tempts my better angel away from my side. She wants to corrupt my saint into a devil, seducing his purity with her foul pride. And whether my angel has been turned into a fiend, I may suspect, but I cannot say for sure. But since both are away from me and friends with each other, I guess that one angel is in the other’s hell. Yet I will never know this for certain, but will live in doubt until my bad angel drives my good one out with fire.
Sonnet 145

Those lips that Love’s own hand made breathed out the words ‘I hate’ to me, who was pining away for her sake. But when she saw how miserable I was, mercy immediately came into her heart. It scolded her tongue, which had always been sweet and used to give gentle judgments. And it taught that tongue to greet me in a new way. She changed ‘I hate’ by adding an ending. It followed the words the way gentle day follows night, which flies away from heaven to hell like a fiend. She threw the hate away from ‘I hate,’ and saved my life by adding ‘not you.’
Sonnet 146

Poor soul, you are the center of my sinful body, and these rebellious desires dress you up. Why do you starve inside and suffer hunger, while you paint your outside walls in such expensive, cheerful colors? Why do you spend so much on your fading mansion, when your lease is so short? Will worms, the heirs of this extravagance, eat up what you have spent? Is that what your body is for? Then, soul, live off your servant the body’s losses, and let it waste away to increase your wealth. Buy long terms in heaven by selling hours of worthless trash. Be fed inside, and stop being rich on the outside. That way you will feed on Death, which feeds on men. And once Death is dead, there will be no more dying.
Sonnet 147

My love is like a fever that keeps longing for the very thing that makes the disease last longer. It feeds on what keeps the illness going, to satisfy its unstable, sickly appetite. My reason, which acted as the doctor for my love, got angry that his prescriptions were not followed and has left me. Now in desperation I find out for myself that desire is death, just as the doctor warned. I am past cure now that Reason no longer cares. I am frantic and mad with endless restlessness. My thoughts and my speech are like a madman’s, wandering randomly from the truth and spoken in vain. For I have sworn that you were fair and thought you bright, when you are as black as hell and as dark as night.
Sonnet 148

Oh, what eyes has Love put in my head, eyes that do not match what is actually there! Or if they do, where has my judgment gone, so that it wrongly condemns what they see correctly? If what my lying eyes dote on is beautiful, what does the world mean by saying it is not? If it is not beautiful, then love clearly shows that a lover’s eye is not as accurate as everyone else’s. No, how could it be? Oh, how can Love’s eye be accurate, when it is so troubled by sleepless watching and by tears? No wonder, then, that I see things wrongly. Even the sun cannot see until the sky clears. Oh, cunning Love! You keep me blind with tears, so that eyes that saw clearly would not find your foul faults.
Sonnet 149

Can you, cruel woman, say that I do not love you, when I take your side against myself? Don’t I think about you when I forget about myself completely for your sake, you tyrant? Who hates you that I call my friend? Whom do you frown on that I flatter? No, if you scowl at me, don’t I immediately take revenge on myself by moaning? What virtue do I value in myself that is so proud it would refuse to serve you? Everything best in me worships your faults and is commanded by a glance of your eyes. But, love, keep hating me, because now I know what you think. You love those who can see clearly, and I am blind.
Sonnet 150

Oh, where do you get this powerful ability to rule my heart with your very shortcomings? Where do you get the power to make me call my own true sight a liar, and swear that brightness does not make the day beautiful? Where do you get this way of making bad things attractive? Even in the worst of your actions there is such strength and guarantee of skill that, in my mind, your worst is better than all the best. Who taught you how to make me love you more, the more I hear and see good reasons to hate you? Oh, though I love what others hate, you should not join others in hating my condition. If your unworthiness made me love you, then I am all the more worthy to be loved by you.
Sonnet 151

Love is too young to know what conscience is. Yet who does not know that conscience is born from love? So, gentle cheater, do not keep pointing out my wrongs, or your sweet self may turn out to be guilty of my faults. For when you betray me, I betray my nobler part, my soul, to the treason of my crude body. My soul tells my body that it may triumph in love. My flesh waits for no further argument. Instead, it rises at the sound of your name and points you out as its prize of triumph. Proud of this swelling, it is content to be your poor slave, to stand up in your affairs and then fall by your side. Do not think it is a lack of conscience that I call her my ‘love,’ for whose dear love I rise and fall.
Sonnet 152

You know that in loving you I have broken my oath. But you have broken two oaths in swearing love to me. In the act of sex you broke your marriage vow, and you tore up your new promise by vowing new hate after feeling new love. But why do I accuse you of breaking two oaths, when I break twenty? I am the worst oath-breaker. All my vows are only oaths that misrepresent you, and all my honest faith in you is lost. I have sworn solemn oaths about your deep kindness, oaths about your love, your truthfulness and your faithfulness. To make you look bright, I made my eyes blind, or made them swear against what they actually see. I have sworn that you are fair. I am all the more a liar for swearing such a foul lie against the truth.

chapters.title: Sonnets 153–154: Cupid
paragraphs: Sonnet 153

Cupid put down his torch and fell asleep. One of Diana’s virgin nymphs found her chance and quickly plunged his love-kindling fire into a cold spring in a valley nearby. The spring took from this holy fire of Love a lively heat that has no end and will last forever. It became a boiling bath, which men still find to be a powerful cure for strange diseases. But Love’s torch was lit again from my mistress’s eye, and the boy decided to test it by touching my heart with it. Sick from that, I wanted the help of the bath and hurried there, a sad, diseased guest. But I found no cure. The bath that can help me is where Cupid got his new fire: my mistress’s eyes.
Sonnet 154

Once the little god of Love lay asleep, with the torch that sets hearts on fire laid down beside him. Meanwhile many nymphs who had sworn to stay chaste came skipping past. The loveliest of these devoted maidens picked up that fire in her virgin hand, the same fire that had warmed legions of faithful hearts. So the commander of hot desire was disarmed in his sleep by a virgin’s hand. She put out the torch in a cool spring nearby. The spring took endless heat from Love’s fire and became a hot bath and a healing cure for sick men. But I, my mistress’s slave, came there to be cured, and this is what I proved by it: Love’s fire heats water, but water does not cool love.
